# ACLU Marks the Supreme Court Term with New Digital Museum Experience Highlighting Landmark SCOTUS Cases


## The People’s Archive offers a dynamic digital journey through pivotal moments in ACLU’s over 100-year history defending civil rights and civil liberties.


October 13, 2026 9:30 am


---


Spokesperson


[Yasmin Cader › ACLU she/her](https://www.aclu.org/bios/yasmin-cader)


Media Contact


media@aclu.org(212) 549-2666


125 Broad Street


18th Floor


New York, NY 10004


United States


NEW YORK – Today, the ACLU launched[The People’s Archive,](https://www.aclu.org/archive) a dynamic digital museum that combines photography, audio, print, and video chronicling the organization’s key civil rights and civil liberties milestones throughout its over 100-year history.


This digital museum experience tells the story of how the ACLU’s pivotal legal cases have helped to defend the Constitution and the very principles upon which our nation was founded 250 years ago. The People’s Archive visitors will also have an opportunity to hear excerpts from some of the ACLU’s landmark arguments before the Supreme Court, including *Speiser v. Randall* (1958), *Engel v. Vitale* (1962 *), Planned Parenthood v. Casey* (1992), *McCreary County v. ACLU of Kentucky* (2005) *, Trump v. Barbara* (2026) *,* and more.


“Democracy grows stronger each time people come together to defend their rights and freedoms,” said **Yasmin Cader, ACLU deputy executive director for program, strategy, and culture** . “The victories we’ve won for civil rights and civil liberties give us a foundation to build on and a responsibility to keep going. As a new Supreme Court term begins, that work continues.”


[The People’s Archive](https://www.aclu.org/archive) highlights the ACLU’s work across decades — from the 1920s to the 2020s – highlighting critical moments where the ACLU intervened when civil rights and civil liberties were at stake, such as racial justice, free speech in schools, reproductive freedom, privacy, and more. It also illustrates how many of the issues the ACLU championed at the time of its founding over a century ago — including free speech, immigration, racial justice, women’s rights — remain under threat today.


The People’s Archive serves as living proof that our nation’s institutions are strong enough to endure periods of devastating rollbacks, the abuse of power, and attacks upon marginalized communities. This digital museum experience will leave visitors with the recognition that, together, the people are stronger than any presidential administration, legal challenge, or dark moment in our nation’s history.


The People’s Archive can be experienced[here](https://www.aclu.org/archive) .
